_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: MISHNA. All sacrificial animals in which a permanent blemish preceded their consecration: they had a permanent blemish, and he consecrated them to be sold, so that an offering for the altar would be brought with their money.
rashi:a1.2: They are obligated in the firstborn: after their redemption, if they gave birth.
rashi:a1.3: And in the gifts: the foreleg, the jaw and the maw, like fully non-sacred animals.
rashi:a1.4: And they emerge to non-sacred status: completely, through their redemption, to be shorn and worked like plain non-sacred animals, because the severe sanctity never took effect on them in the first place.
rashi:a1.5: And one who slaughters them outside is exempt: even before their redemption. Even if their blemish is a minor one, such as pale spots in the eye, for which one who slaughters ordinary sacrificial animals outside is liable, here he is exempt, because so great a sanctity never took effect on them in the first place.
rashi:a2.1: And they do not render a substitute: this is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:a2.2: And if they died: before their redemption, they are redeemed in order to feed them to the dogs, since their sanctity is not severe. And it further teaches us that they are lesser than other sacrificial animals, which are redeemed only alive, so that they can stand before the priest at the time of their valuation, as it is written: “Then he shall stand the animal [before the priest],” and afterward, “And the priest shall appraise it” (Leviticus 27:11–12).
rashi:a2.3: Except for the firstborn and the tithe: for even with their blemish the severe sanctity takes effect on them. The firstborn, because the womb sanctifies it; and of the tithe it is written: “He shall not inquire whether it be good or bad” (Leviticus 27:33), which implies that whether it is unblemished or blemished it is sacred: “good” is unblemished, “bad” is blemished.
rashi:a3.1: A temporary blemish: it is as though it were not there, and sanctity takes effect on them.
rashi:a3.2: Exempt from the firstborn: this is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:a3.3: And they do not emerge, etc.: for even after their redemption they are forbidden in shearing and labor, as the Gemara explains.
rashi:a4.1: Their offspring and their milk are prohibited, etc.: the Gemara explains: where they became pregnant before their redemption and gave birth after their redemption.
rashi:a4.2: And one who slaughters them outside: before their redemption.
rashi:a4.3: Is liable: to karet. And in the Gemara it is explained as referring to pale spots in the eye, which are fit [to be brought] inside, and in accordance with Rabbi Akiva, who says that if they were brought up [onto the altar] they are not taken down. But with other blemishes, no, for we say in Tractate Yoma (63b): Whatever is fit for the Tent of Meeting, one is liable for it; if not, not.
rashi:a4.4: They must be buried: and they are not redeemed, because they require standing and valuation.
rashi:a5.1: GEMARA. The reason is that they were redeemed: this refers to the first clause.
rashi:a5.2: Sanctity of value: exempts from the firstborn just like inherent sanctity, as is explained below from verses that it exempts from the firstborn and from the gifts.
rashi:a6.1: Items consecrated for Temple maintenance, etc.: and these are like items consecrated for Temple maintenance, since they themselves were consecrated from the outset only for their value.
rashi:a7.1: No: do not bring support from our mishna. Here it is sanctity of value for the altar, for they were consecrated for that purpose, that their money be offered on the altar, and there it is forbidden in shearing and labor because it can be confused with inherent sanctity for the altar.
rashi:a9.1: But [before their redemption]: offspring born before their redemption are forbidden in benefit without redemption. And they are not offered, since they come from the force of a deferred sanctity, for their mother was not consecrated for the altar [itself].
tosafot:a1.1: All sacrificial animals in which a permanent blemish preceded their consecration: this does not speak of items consecrated for Temple maintenance, but of one who consecrated them for the altar, for their value. For there is no difference between the first clause and the latter clause except that in this one the blemish preceded the consecration and in that one the consecration preceded the blemish. And although one transgresses when he consecrates a blemished animal for the altar, as we say in the first chapter of Temura (6b), in any case the mishna teaches us its law. And there the Gemara asks how this differs from [consecrating] a mere palm tree, and answers: the matter is more pointed, since he passes over unblemished animals and consecrates blemished ones.
tosafot:a5.1: Sanctity of value defers from the firstborn and from the gifts: the Kuntres [Rashi] explained: sanctity of value exempts from the firstborn like inherent sanctity, as is explained below from verses that it exempts from the firstborn and from the gifts. This is difficult for his explanation, for there we exempt disqualified consecrated animals even though they were redeemed, since they are compared to the gazelle and the deer, whereas here [the exemption is] specifically when they were not redeemed. Rather, this is the reason with sanctity of value: because regarding the firstborn it is written “in Israel” (Numbers 3:13), and regarding the gifts it is written “from the people” (Deuteronomy 18:3).
gershom:a1.1: And they emerge to non-sacred status to be shorn and worked: even though other disqualified consecrated animals are forbidden in shearing and labor, since the blemish preceded the consecration, these are permitted.
gershom:a2.1: And their offspring and their milk are permitted after their redemption: this is why benefit from it is permitted after their redemption: even though it was conceived before their redemption, since it was born after their redemption, it is permitted without redemption.
gershom:a3.1: And one who slaughters them outside: outside the Temple courtyard.
gershom:a4.1: And they do not render a substitute: even before their redemption.
gershom:a5.1: Except for the firstborn and the tithe: for even though a permanent blemish preceded their consecration [they are fully sacred]. [The printed text is garbled here; the editor’s correction reads “preceded”.]
gershom:a6.1: And they were redeemed: in any case their law is like that of sacrificial animals, and they are exempt from the firstborn and the gifts, because their sanctity came of itself and it is inherent sanctity. And if you say: with a firstborn, how can a blemish precede its consecration, when its sanctity is from the womb? For example, where it was blemished in its mother’s womb, before the exit from the womb sanctified it.
gershom:a7.1: Sanctity of value defers from the firstborn and from the gifts: since a permanent blemish preceded their consecration, that consecration is only sanctity of value, that they be sold and sacrificial animals brought with their money. And even so, if they are not redeemed they are exempt from the firstborn and from the gifts.
gershom:a8.1: Items consecrated for Temple maintenance: they are sanctity of value, to be sold for the needs of the Temple’s repair.
gershom:a9.1: Forbidden in shearing and labor: before their redemption.
gershom:a10.1: They said: No. In any case it does not support Rabbi Eliezer. For this is the reason of the tanna of our mishna, who forbids them in shearing and labor when they were not redeemed: these, which were consecrated with their blemish, are sanctity of value for the altar, that they be sold and unblemished offerings brought for the altar with their money; and if you permit them in shearing and labor, people will come to confuse them and permit [the same] with sanctity of the altar. Items consecrated for Temple maintenance, which are not sanctity of value for the altar and cannot be confused, the Rabbis did not decree to be forbidden in shearing and labor. So in any case it does not support him.
gershom:a11.1: But before: where they were conceived and born before their redemption, those offspring are forbidden without redemption.
rashi:b1.1: Are they redeemed unblemished: those offspring that were born before their redemption; or are they not redeemed unblemished?
rashi:b2.2: Primary: the mother. Evidently they are redeemed unblemished.
rashi:b3.1: And the Gemara infers: the reason it does not require a blemish is that the subsidiary should not be more stringent than the primary, since they come from the force of a blemished animal. But animals that do not come from the force of a blemished animal, but one consecrates them themselves for their value, do not go out to non-sacred status without a blemish, for they are sanctified with inherent sanctity.
rashi:b3.3: He consecrated a male for its value: that he would sell it and bring a burnt offering with its money; it itself is sanctified with inherent sanctity and is offered as a burnt offering. That is why it says “male”: because it is fit for a burnt offering, for most people who bring an offering bring a burnt offering.
tosafot:b3.1: He consecrated a male for its value; it is sanctified with inherent sanctity: that is why it says “male,” because it itself is offered as a burnt offering. Had it said simply “an animal,” I would have said that a female too is sanctified with inherent sanctity and is offered as a peace offering. And we hear from Rabbi Yehoshua in Tractate Shekalim (6a), cited in Temura, chapter Elu Kodashim (Temura 20a), regarding one who consecrates his property: the males themselves are offered as burnt offerings, and the females are sold for the needs of peace offerings and burnt offerings are brought with their money. However, it seems that for Rabbi Eliezer too, who says there that the males are sold for the needs of burnt offerings and the females are sold for the needs of peace offerings, and their money goes with the rest of the property to Temple maintenance, and according to what Rava wanted to say at first there in that chapter, that one who consecrates a male is not sanctified with inherent sanctity, there is no difficulty at all from the mishna in Shekalim: one can distinguish between one who consecrates his property without specifying and one who stated explicitly “for its value.”
rashi:b4.1: Rabbi Elazar teaches: one who slaughters outside is liable. He does not mean karet but lashes.
rashi:b4.2: And he interprets: this “outside” as, for example, where he slaughtered it on a private altar at the time when private altars were permitted.
rashi:b5.1: A private altar: that each and every one builds an altar for himself, such as the altars of Manoaḥ, Gideon and Samuel.
rashi:b5.2: A great altar: Nov and Givon, which belonged to the public.
rashi:b6.1: Since it is sanctified when it is blemished: to be forbidden in shearing and labor.
rashi:b8.1: And say: if it is not relevant, etc.: and in fact [the verse speaks of] the great altar.
rashi:b8.2: He shall not inquire: he shall not examine between unblemished and blemished, for whichever is tenth shall be sacred.
rashi:b9.1: He derives “passing”, “passing” from the firstborn: just as a blemished firstborn is not offered, so too a blemished tithe is not. When the verse comes, it comes for a private altar.
rashi:b10.1: He shall not exchange it, a good for a bad: that is, a blemished one; “if he shall at all substitute, it shall be holy,” even a blemished one.
rashi:b12.1: Offspring: blemished ones born of unblemished sacrificial animals.
rashi:b13.1: The tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael has already ruled: from another verse, and this one is not needed for that.
rashi:b13.2: Only your sacred items, etc.: these are the substitutes: it comes to teach us that they are offered on the altar. For if it came for the principal consecration, why do I need it written that one should bring them up to Jerusalem? We already know that from many verses: “Take heed to yourself lest you offer your burnt offerings,” etc. (Deuteronomy 12:13).
rashi:b13.4: So too these, when blemished, are not: therefore, when “You shall not sacrifice” comes, it comes for a private altar.
tosafot:b9.1: He derives “passing”: he could have said [a verbal analogy of] “in place of”, “in place of” from sacrificial animals; but because the tithe and the firstborn are alike in several matters, he chose it.
tosafot:b13.1: He juxtaposed them to vows: this is not part of the baraita in Temura, chapter Elu Kodashim (Temura 17b); Rava explains it so on his own. And below (Bekhorot 15b), in our discussion, there is another baraita that derives substitutes and offspring from “male or female,” and it disagrees with the tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael here, as explained in Temura (17b), and so Rashi explained below. That tanna too derives it well: the verse juxtaposed substitutes and offspring to the body of the offering, since “whether male or female” speaks of the body of the offering, except that from the extra wording we also expound substitutes and offspring. And on this view the juxtaposition above, which compares its substitute to it, is no longer needed.
rashi:b14.1: Now that you have said bad for good is not: that he should not bring unblemished non-sacred animals beside a blemished sacred animal and say: This is the substitute of that.
rashi:b14.2: Rather: that is why “good for bad” is written.
rashi:b14.3: Good at the outset: one that was caught in sanctity when it was unblemished makes a substitute even though it became blemished, as it is written: “or a bad for a good,” which implies a bad sacred animal for a good non-sacred one: a bad sacred animal makes a substitute.
tosafot:b14.1: In brief: Is it necessary to state good for bad? This discussion is from the first chapter of Temura (9a). There Rava holds that one does not derive a prohibition from an a fortiori inference and expounds the verse another way, while Abaye does not count this as an inference at all; here the Gemara takes Abaye’s derivation because it is plainer. Similarly in Sanhedrin (34b), on “one examines leprous marks only by day,” the Gemara brings Abaye’s derivation (“by day, and not by night”) and leaves aside Rava’s (from “to me, and not to my light”). One should not wonder at Elu Nisrafin (Sanhedrin 76a), where it seems the reverse with regard to one’s daughter from a woman he raped, derived a fortiori from his daughter’s daughter, which Abaye treats as merely revealing the meaning. There the two cases are not learned from each other: with regard to one’s sister a verse was needed by all opinions for a father’s daughter and a mother’s daughter, since one does not derive a prohibition a fortiori, and it is not treated as merely revealing the meaning because the plain sense of the verse, “his father’s daughter or his mother’s daughter,” implies that it comes to exclude. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b14.2: Is it necessary to state good for bad? And if you say: perhaps it was needed because of the end of the verse, “then both it and that for which it is substituted shall be holy”? One may say that it could have written that in its latter part: “And if he shall at all substitute good for bad or bad for good.”
rashi:b15.1: This is the statement of Rabbi Shimon: who says in the last chapter of Temura (32a): Items consecrated for the altar were included in standing and valuation.
rashi:b16.1: As we learned: Rabbi Shimon says, etc.: since Rabbi Shimon says that items consecrated for Temple maintenance were not included, by implication the verse is written about items consecrated for the altar; and here he concedes regarding one blemished from the outset that it is redeemed, even though it is consecrated for the altar. And from where do we know that the tanna of our mishna holds that items consecrated for the altar were included in standing and valuation, which require that they be alive at the time of redemption, as it is written, “Then he shall stand the animal before the priest,” and afterward, “and the priest shall appraise it”? From what it teaches in the latter clause about animals whose consecration preceded their blemish [that they must be buried], since when he consecrated them for the altar he consecrated them unblemished.
tosafot:b16.1: In brief: And Rabbi Shimon concedes regarding one blemished from the outset. According to what is said shortly (15a), that Rav holds like Reish Lakish, who says that according to the Rabbis items consecrated for the altar were not included in standing and valuation, it is well that Rabbi Shimon “concedes” to the Rabbis. But according to the conclusion that Rav holds like Rabbi Yoḥanan, that according to the Rabbis both kinds were included, to whom does he concede? One may explain that it says this so that you should not think the reason of our mishna is that one does not redeem in order to feed dogs, and not standing and valuation, as though items for the altar did not need standing and valuation, which is why in the first clause, where the blemish came first, they are redeemed. It teaches us that the reason of the mishna is standing and valuation, as the Gemara soon infers from the fact that it does not teach “and if they became tereifa”; and in the first clause, where the blemish came first, Rabbi Shimon concedes that standing and valuation are not required. Since one might err and think he disagrees with the mishna, it had to say that he concedes it. And it names Rabbi Shimon because for him it is more obvious that items for the altar were included in standing and valuation: since he says items for Temple maintenance were not, the verse must be speaking of items for the altar. For the Rabbis it is not so obvious, since one could say they were not included, as Reish Lakish says. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b16.2: “It,” to exclude one blemished from the outset: all items consecrated for Temple maintenance, according to Rabbi Shimon, we exclude from another verse, at the end of Temura (33a).
rashi:b17.1: But the Rabbis: not those Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Shimon in Tractate Temura, for there we say that according to all, one blemished from the outset was not included in standing and valuation. Rather, it is the tanna of the school of Levi.
rashi:b18.1: Even an undomesticated animal: which is not fit for the altar.
rashi:b19.1: So too, if they died they are redeemed: since they concede regarding one blemished from the outset.
gershom:b1.1: Are they redeemed unblemished: those offspring.
gershom:b2.1: Or are they not redeemed unblemished: so that one must wait with them until they become blemished, and afterward redeem them.
gershom:b3.1: Rav Amram taught: [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text reads “Rav Amram taught” where ours reads “Come and hear.”] One who dedicates permanently blemished animals for the altar: that is, where their blemish preceded their consecration, and they gave birth before their redemption. They may be sold and they do not require a blemish: there is no need to wait with those offspring and not sell them until a blemish befalls them.
gershom:b4.1: [That they are not imbued with sanctity:] because these come from the force of a deferred sanctity.
gershom:b5.1: That the subsidiary should not: the offspring, which are sanctified only by virtue of their mother.
gershom:b6.1: Be more stringent than the primary: than their mother. Rather, just as their mother can be redeemed at any time, so too their offspring are redeemed whenever he wishes, even unblemished. Evidently they are redeemed unblemished. And now he infers from the baraita: the reason they are redeemed unblemished is that the subsidiary should not be more stringent; but if he consecrated an unblemished male for its value, even though he said, “I consecrate it only for its value,” it is sanctified with inherent sanctity, since it is fit to be offered, and it is not redeemed unblemished. And though it says “but if he consecrated an unblemished male,” the same is true of a female; it says “male” here only because it wants to support Rava, and Rava speaks only of a male, as is said in Temura, chapter Elu Kodashim: Rava said: That is to say, one who consecrates a male, etc.
gershom:b7.1: And he interprets it as a private altar: and all the more so he is liable at a public altar. And that is why it calls it “outside,” since there is no courtyard there. And he is liable because he offers a blemished animal at an altar at the time when private altars were permitted. And when were they permitted? As we say: When they came to Nov and Givon, private altars were permitted, etc.
gershom:b8.1: Say: expound this “You shall not sacrifice” thus: if it is not relevant to sacrificial animals, for it is already written: “Blind or broken,” etc.
gershom:b9.1: Apply it to the matter of a firstborn, for it might enter your mind: since it is sanctified with its blemish of itself when it is born blemished, [I would say] it is also offered with its blemish. “You shall not sacrifice” teaches us that it is not, and then it would not come for a private altar.
gershom:b10.1: They said, etc.: and “You shall not sacrifice” remains free for a private altar.
gershom:b11.1: Since it is sanctified with its blemish: of itself, when it passes under the rod, as it is written: “He shall not inquire whether it be good or bad”; “bad” means a blemished animal, as is said below.
gershom:b12.1: Since it is sanctified when it is blemished, as it is written: “He shall not exchange it…a good for a bad; and if he shall at all substitute,” etc.
gershom:b13.1: Since they are sanctified [by virtue of] their mother when they are blemished: whether they were born blemished or it happened to them afterward.
gershom:b14.1: Rava said: The tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael has already ruled, etc. And “You shall not sacrifice” remains free for a private altar, as Rabbi Elazar says.
gershom:b15.1: Now, bad for good: to exchange a blemished animal for an unblemished one.
gershom:b16.1: You have said no: at the outset; but after the fact, “then both it and that for which it is substituted shall be holy.”
gershom:b17.1: Good for bad: is it necessary to state that unblemished for blemished is not permitted at the outset?
gershom:b18.1: Rather: this “good for bad” comes only to teach us that for a good-for-bad exchange to make a substitute after the fact, we require [the consecrated animal] to be good at the outset, its consecration having preceded its blemish. But one that is bad at the outset, whose blemish preceded its consecration, never makes a substitute.
gershom:b19.1: And if they died: before their redemption, they are redeemed, and benefit from their hide and carcass is permitted.
gershom:b20.1: [This is the statement of Rabbi Shimon:] the tanna of our mishna, who says “if they died they are redeemed”: this is the statement of Rabbi Shimon, who says in Tractate Temura, in the last chapter: Items consecrated for the altar were included in standing [and valuation], etc., but not items consecrated for Temple maintenance, which are sanctity of value and do not require standing.
gershom:b21.1: And Rabbi Shimon concedes regarding one blemished from the outset: before consecration. For even though items consecrated for the altar require standing and valuation, on this one, blemished from the outset, full consecration for the altar did not take effect. Therefore, even if they died, when one cannot stand them, they are redeemed, for it is sanctity of value and its law is like that of items consecrated for Temple maintenance, which were not included in standing and valuation.
gershom:b22.1: And the Rabbis say: if they died they must be buried: even one blemished from the outset, for they hold that all were included in standing and valuation. Therefore, since they died and one cannot stand them, they are not subject to redemption; rather, they must be buried. And these Rabbis are not Rabbi Shimon’s disputants who disagree with him in Temura, but other Rabbis: the tanna of the school of Levi, who is stringent regarding one blemished from the outset.
gershom:b23.1: But isn’t it written “it”? That is to say: “it” requires standing and valuation, which excludes one blemished from the outset that died, which is redeemed even though it cannot stand. It is difficult.
gershom:b24.1: But the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Shimon in Tractate Temura, who say that both items consecrated for the altar and items consecrated for Temple maintenance were included in standing and valuation, and who concede that animals blemished from the outset are redeemed: so too would they be redeemed after death?
gershom:b25.1: If so: let him say: This is the statement of Rabbi Shimon and those who disagree with him.
